headline: High: shared filesystem and B's write/network defaults create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risk; A is read-only but can still be a content source.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no network egress and no I/O surfaces, so it cannot directly ingest B. But B can read/write files and spawn subprocesses, so if A's outputs are placed in a shared workspace or copied into documents, B may treat attacker-controlled content as instructions. The pathway is plausible from the profiles, though not documented end-to-end.
conditions: IF A's outputs are copied into files that B later parses as instructions
IF A and B share a writable workspace or clipboard bridge
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate directories
Disable automatic instruction-following on parsed documents
Add a provenance header to A's outputs
Review any B-ingested file before execution
requires-engineering: enforce content-type separation in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no egress, but B processes documents/images/text and has allowlisted network egress plus filesystem access. If both agents share a workspace, B can read files produced by A and transmit extracted content to its backend or APIs. The pairwise leakage path is therefore plausible in default document-processing setups, though A itself is not a data source.
conditions: IF A writes artifacts containing sensitive text into a directory B can read
IF B processes those artifacts with network egress enabled
mitigations: Store A and B outputs in separate folders
Turn off B network egress for sensitive runs
Redact sensitive fields before B ingests files
Limit B to a read-only copy of inputs
requires-engineering: add per-file access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A is effectively non-runnable and has no write or network capabilities, while B can write the filesystem, install packages, and spawn subprocesses. There is no direct write-write conflict from A, but if an orchestrator maps A's artifacts into B's mutable workspace, B can overwrite or mutate shared files. Uncertainty about A's runtime surface pushes this above low.
conditions: IF the orchestrator places A and B in the same writable directory
IF B is allowed to modify files that A produced
mitigations: Use separate working directories
Mount A outputs read-only for B
Serialize any shared-file access
Pin B package installs to an isolated environment
requires-engineering: add lockfiles or transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a sample integration repo and B is a document processor; if A's generated content is fed into B, B may render or act on it without verification. B's document-processing role makes it likely to transform A's outputs into downstream artifacts, so a bad instruction or malformed content from A can cascade. A lacks action authority, so this is not high, but the default pipeline risk is real.
conditions: IF B consumes A's output as authoritative input
IF no validation step checks A's content before B transforms it
mitigations: Insert a validation step between A and B
Require human review of A-generated artifacts
Reject unexpected markup or commands in A outputs
Log and diff B inputs before processing
requires-engineering: add schema validation for the handoff

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no declared PHI, residency, or retention commitments. B exposes privacy-policy and docs URLs, but there is no evidence of a compliance mismatch with A. Because the profiles are sparse and unverified, I keep this at low rather than none, but the pairwise compliance pathway is not demonstrated.
conditions: IF either agent is later configured to handle regulated data
IF B's privacy-policy terms conflict with the operator's obligations
mitigations: Confirm data-class handling before deployment
Avoid regulated data in this pair
Review B privacy-policy terms
Document retention settings
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls
